revisions.title: Before the speech: a forecast of enchantment
revisions.body: Menexenus has come from the council-chamber because the speaker for the war dead will be chosen tomorrow; no oration has yet been heard in this scene. Socrates therefore offers a forecast, imagining prepared praise making him feel greater, nobler, and more beautiful. Menexenus punctures the performance by calling it Socrates’ habitual mockery of the orators.

revisions.title: A speech with shifting attributions
revisions.body: Read this opening as a chain of attributions, not a settled account of authorship. Socrates reports Aspasia as his rhetoric teacher and says he heard her going through a funeral speech; he only conjectures that she had assembled some earlier parts from remnants of Pericles’ speech. What follows is therefore presented as remembered, attributed material. Menexenus even allows Socrates to call it Aspasia’s—or anyone’s. The privacy remark frames a playful promise to gratify him, not an exclusive condition of the speech.

revisions.title: When the copy claims priority
revisions.body: The speech’s decisive move is not the comparison of earth and woman but its reversal of who copies whom. By making the earth the model and woman the imitator, it turns a familiar maternal analogy into a claim of priority: Athenian earth is presented as the original, while human birth repeats its pattern. Read this as rhetorical persuasion, not demonstrated metaphysics.

revisions.title: From common birth to civic equality
revisions.body: The oration builds civic equality from a claimed common origin. It presents Athens as an aristocracy approved by the multitude, with rule assigned to those deemed wise or good, then moves from equality of birth to equality before the law. The image of citizens as brothers from one mother is the premise of that legal reciprocity, not its result: because they share a civic origin, they refuse to be one another’s masters or slaves, yielding only to recognized virtue and understanding.

revisions.title: External victories, internal defeat
revisions.body: The catalogue changes direction here. After listing victories and losses in Sicily and the Hellespont, the speaker marks the Greek appeal to Persia as the war’s unexpected turn. He then uses the rescuers’ victory to present Athens as unconquerable from without, while locating defeat in internal dissension. I read that last move as the oration’s framing of defeat, not as a conclusion the passage independently proves.

revisions.title: Civic kinship becomes public ritual
revisions.body: The passage invites us to hear civic care as a replacement kinship: the city takes the position of heir and son to the dead, father to the orphans, and guardian to their parents. Annual rites and contests give that care an institutional form. Then the imperative to depart snaps the consolatory picture back into public procedure.
